decisions.reason: The candidate already has a complete same-message MODIFY covering hidden liquid traps, removable cleaning components, sanitation, and retail-use scope; liquid-electrical separation remains owned by the source Requirement.
Liquid-electrical separation and sanitation considerations do not change the required dispensing flow, consistency preservation, or pour direction.
The separation constraint does not alter the selected solenoid mechanism, button actuation behavior, or pre-dispense isolation semantics.
The source decision does not change the spout location, orientation, fabrication style, geometry reference, or pour direction.
The candidate already has a same-message MODIFY extending the established whisk-removal behavior to sanitation and retail-use contexts.
The candidate already has a complete same-message MODIFY establishing food-safe contact materials and sanitation and retail-use scope.
The candidate already has a same-message MODIFY extending the existing bowl-removal behavior to cleaning, sanitation, and retail-use contexts.
Food-service sanitation and liquid-electrical separation do not replace or modify the existing V1 component-sourcing strategy.

The client explicitly places accessibility for maintenance and component replacement among the considerations for prospective retail use, extending the existing service-access Requirement to that context.

source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
Hey Larry, The latest updates are looking great. Seeing the plumbing, drainage routing, bowl integration, and overall structure come together has me even more excited about where this is heading. As I’ve been thinking ahead, one thing that keeps coming to mind is the possibility of eventually using the Matcha Mixer in a retail location if we move forward with opening a shop. Because of that, I wanted to start thinking about food-service and health department considerations early while we’re still in the prototype stage. A few things I’d love to keep in mind as the build progresses: 
 Food-contact materials (stainless steel, food-grade plastics, food-grade silicone, etc.) Ease of cleaning and sanitation Making sure there aren’t any hidden areas where liquid can collect or become trapped Easy removal of bowls, whisks, and components for cleaning Separation between liquids and electrical components Accessibility for maintenance and servicing if something ever needs to be replaced When you get a chance, I’d also love to know what materials are being used in the food-contact areas and whether there are any areas you see as potential sanitation or cleaning challenges. Long term, I think it would be helpful to keep documentation on: 
 materials used CAD files wiring layout cleaning procedures exploded-view drawings if available Not because we need all of that right now, but because if this evolves into something bigger, having that information could be incredibly valuable. Overall, everything is looking fantastic and I’m really excited to see the testing videos and final assembly. It’s amazing seeing the project move from an idea into a real machine. 

Karla Burton

decisions.reason: The physical separation requirement does not change the 120V input source, battery policy, power capacity, controller capacity, or reserve margin.
The source adds a containment and electrical-separation constraint but does not modify the candidate's repeated-operation reliability or electrical-load capacity.
The sanitation and liquid-electrical separation decision does not alter bowl capacity, form, selected size, or capacity-selection priorities.
